newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: INTERVIEW - PRAGUE BOURSE CHIEF ON MARKET REGULATION.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - PRAGUE BOURSE CHIEF ON MARKET REGULATION.

text.p: Prague Stock Exchange Chairman Tomas Jezek will meet with Prime Minister Vaclav Klaus and key economic ministers on Sunday to discuss problems in the regulation and supervision of the Czech capital markets.

Jezek has been an outspoken proponent for the creation of an independent U.S.-style Securities and Exchange Commission to take over regulation of securities trading from the Finance Ministry, over the objections of senior ministry officials.

Jezek met with Reuters Prague correspondent John Mastrini to discuss the prospects for re-regulating the markets -- which investors have widely complained are lacking transparency and are racked with insider trading.

JEZEK: The stock exchange chamber is determined to do its best for enhancing transparency and disclosure. We've internally declared simply that time of the transition to a standard regime is over in December this year.

Begining next year we will behave very strictly and we will not tolerate what has been tolerated before. The Prague Stock Exchange and the capital markets are three years old, and three years for learning is more than enough.
The problem is that not all brokers are members of the stock exchange so and any disciplinary measures and any hardening of rules can be applied to exchange members only.

We absolutely need the collaboration of the ministry of finance which is responsible for the capital markets as a whole. For this reason we have invited (Finance Minister Ivan) Kocarnik to extraordinary sessions of the stock exchange chamber.

My general conclusion is that the capital markets cannot be deeply transformed or enhanced within the existing institutional framework -- I mean the existing supervisory authority (the finance ministry).

So I have taken the strategic decision to do everything necessary for the establishement of a Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) in the Czech Republic. I hope that this commission should start to operate from July of next year.

The talks on the project are going very well right now, following the time schedule, but the problem is what will happen in the meantime. Up to now the Ministry of Finance is responsible for supervision and everybody you meet in the market, regardless if its a foreign investor or small investor from voucher privatisation, everybody is dissatisfied and full of criticism against the performance of the ministry of finance.

The standardisation of the institutional framework, in other words the creation of the Czech SEC is the solution. I'm not so naive that I believe the problems will just disappear, but it should open the chances for the Czech capital markets.
Without the SEC the Czech capital markets have no chance. The SEC would play the same role and would have approximately the same powers as the U.S. SEC.
REUTERS: Knowing the (negative) opinions of the Finance Ministry toward your plan, do you feel you can achieve the support which is necessary?

JEZEK: It could be better, but I do not rely on their (the Finance Ministry's) support, exclusively. Who I am relying on is the budget committee and the parliament. We are supported by the parliament and the parliament is ready to adopt the necessary legislation.
REUTERS:So you expect this legilsation would be submitted by the budget committee not by the Finance Ministry, meaning it will not be a government proposal.
JEZEK: It would be better if it would be a government proposal, but I'm a little bit skeptical about it. I think the second best solution is through the intiative of a group of deputies.
REUTERS: You are working with Wood & Company and other market participants to help create the SEC who is involved in this?

JEZEK: We are working with a British consultancy firm -- Milford International -- together with U.S. AID (Agency for International Development) who will provide us with a final reading, a final criticism of the plan. U.S. AID is represented by Robert Smith, the former SEC chairman.

Two members of the budget committee are members of my working group -- the chairman Mr. (Jozef) Wagner (of the opposition Social Democrats) and the chairman of the subcommittee on (securities) controls and supervision Mr. Tomas Pav (of the ruling Civic Democratic Party).
REUTERS: The central bank has suggested this umbrella organisation which would oversee all the regulatory agencies in the economy.
JEZEK: I would be fine, but I have not seen anything concrete.
REUTERS: Was it only a suggestion then, nothing concrete?
JEZEK: Yes, no written or concrete steps have been taken.

REUTERS: Have you discussed this at all with (central bank) Governor (Josef) Tosovsky. Yes, I met with him. I am supported by him and it doesn't seem that there is any question on the creation of some umbrella organisation. It will have separate activities (apart from the Czech SEC), pulling together the SEC and banking supervision.
REUTERS: The SEC as you see it would be fully independent or a quasi-government agency.
JEZEK: It would be fully independent, financed through transaction fees on a percentage basis or a lump sum.
REUTERS: Do you have any estimate what would be the transaction fee?
JEZEK: No, not yet. We have estimated, but its very rough and shouldn't be said.
REUTERS: Can you qualify what is the biggest problem among all the complaints about a lack of transparency on the Czech capital markets?

JEZEK: The biggest problem... Everybody speaks about a lack of transparency, but the biggest problem is that one share has two prices. One price officially produced by the stock exchange, by the conduct of trades but what is growing is the percentage of trades off the stock exchange which typically does not produce a price. So the first step toward transparency is the obligatory disclosure in real-time of prices realised on OTC (off-market) trades, and here we need absolutely to cooperation of the minister of finance because the majority of brokers are not members of the stock exchange. The existence of double prices on one stock is the source of manipulation and bribes, and corruption.
REUTERS: You will be taking action though before the new legislation passes within the bourse's current structure?
JEZEK: The obligatory disclosure (of OTC) prices will be established (for exchange members), but the rest of the field must be covered by the ministry of finance.
REUTERS: There have been a lot of complaints which also centre on the disclosure of company information?

JEZEK: Yes, but there is some enertia in this respect. It is not perfect, it is getting better, and better. Now is much better than one year ago, and we are doing our best, and it is measurably and visibly better, and getting better every month. Once more it is far from perfect, but I don't see it as a strategic problem, it must be cultivated. We must be patient and put the pressure on the companies.
REUTERS: When you say that the company information disclosure is getting better, do you mean that in terms of quality or timing.
JEZEK: Quality, timing, and frequency. Once more, I do not say that it is okay, but these problems are of a type that can be solved by the stock exchange itself.
-- Prague Newsroom, 42-2-2423-0003
